PAPER: JHSMR Original Article Journal of Health Science and Medical Research Risk Factors of Breakthrough Urinary Tract Infection in Children with Primary Vesicoureteral Reflux Chompearl Wiraseranee, M.D., Pokket Sirisreetreerux, M.D., Wit Viseshsindh, M.D. Division of Urology, Department of Surgery, Faculty of Medicine Ramathibodi Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok 10400, Thailand. Received 10 January 2025 l Revised 12 February 2025 l Accepted 1 March 2025 l Published online 11 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is a significant risk factor for urinary tract infections (UTI) in children, potentially leading to renal damage. Antibiotic prophylaxis is essential for the pediatric patients with VUR aiming to reduce the chance of UTI. However, breakthroughs UTI can occurred despite adequate prophylactic antibiotics. We aimed to identify the factors contributing to breakthrough UTIs in the patients with VUR. Material and Methods: This retrospective study analyzed medical records from 238 children with primary VUR from 2000-2019. This study included children aged less than 10 years old at the time of VUR diagnosis and excluded those with secondary VUR, incomplete medical records, or lost to follow-up. Univariate and multivariate analyses were utilized to determine the predictors of breakthrough UTIs. Results: This study comprised 238 children diagnosed with VUR, including 133 males and 105 females; 86 patients experienced a breakthrough infection. Multivariate analysis revealed that each additional UTI before prophylactic antibiotics significantly increased the likelihood of breakthrough infections (OR 1.62; 95% CI 1.10-2.37; p-value=0.013). Upper pole renal scarring and generalized abnormal renal scans were also significant risk factors with OR 5.57; 95% CI (2.16-14.40); p-value<0.001 and OR 5.19; 95% CI (1.36-19.75); p-value=0.016, respectively. Bowel bladder symptoms emerged as a substantial risk factor (OR 30.16; 95% CI 1.43-633.86; p-value=0.028), whereas the use of cephalexin appeared protective (OR 0.22; 95% CI 0.05-0.94; p-value=0.042). Conclusion: The number of UTIs before prophylaxis antibiotics, abnormal renal scan at the upper pole and generalized kidney and bowel bladder symptoms were independent risk factors for breakthrough infections. Moreover, the study showed that the use of cephalexin was a statistically significant protective factor against breakthrough UTI. JSON: Name: breakthrough_uti_vur_predictors Title: Multivariable and causal-inference analysis of predictors of breakthrough febrile urinary tract infection in children with primary vesicoureteral reflux Short Hypothesis: In children with primary VUR receiving continuous antibiotic prophylaxis, bowel–bladder dysfunction, abnormal DMSA renal scarring localized to the upper pole or with generalized distribution, and a greater number of UTIs before prophylaxis each independently increase the probability of breakthrough febrile UTI, whereas prophylaxis with cephalexin independently decreases that probability. Related Work: Observational cohort studies and clinical trials have examined risk factors and prophylaxis effectiveness in pediatric VUR. Randomized trials demonstrated that continuous prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole reduces recurrence risk relative to placebo in selected populations, while multiple retrospective series associated abnormal renal scintigraphy (DMSA) findings, higher VUR grade, and bowel–bladder dysfunction with recurrent or breakthrough infections. Existing work is limited by heterogeneous antibiotic regimens, inconsistent DMSA reporting (often binary scar/no-scar rather than anatomical localization), variable adjustment for confounders, few studies using causal-inference methods to compare antibiotic agents, and limited external validation of multivariable risk models. Direct comparisons between specific prophylactic agents under real-world prescribing choices are underpowered or confounded by indication. Time-to-event analyses and ablation of individual predictor contributions are rarely reported, leaving uncertainty about independent effects and relative predictive value of DMSA localization, BBD, prior UTI burden, and antibiotic choice. Abstract: Problem: Breakthrough febrile urinary tract infection (UTI) occurs in a subset of children with primary vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) despite continuous antibiotic prophylaxis; predictors and protective prophylactic agents remain incompletely characterized. Approach: Using a retrospective cohort of pediatric primary VUR patients (n=238), we will perform multivariable logistic regression, time-to-event Cox modeling, and causal-inference analyses (propensity-score matching and inverse-probability weighting) to quantify independent associations between clinical variables and breakthrough febrile UTI. Main contribution: We provide anatomically specific DMSA-derived predictors (upper-pole versus generalized scarring), quantify the incremental effect of pre-prophylaxis UTI count, evaluate bowel–bladder dysfunction as an independent risk factor, and compare the real-world effectiveness of cephalexin versus other prophylactic agents using causal methods. Expected outcome: A validated prognostic model and adjusted effect estimates that clarify which children are at elevated risk of breakthrough infection and whether cephalexin offers a protective effect relative to standard agents, informing risk stratification and hypothesis generation for prospective evaluation. Experiments: Datasets: Primary retrospective cohort of children with primary VUR diagnosed by VCUG at a single tertiary center between 2000–2019 (n=238; inclusion: age <10 at diagnosis, primary VUR, ≥1 year follow-up; exclusion: secondary VUR, incomplete records). If available, external validation cohort from an independent center or split-sample validation (70% train, 30% test) and 5-fold cross-validation. Input variables: age, sex, BMI, number of UTIs before prophylaxis (count), eGFR, VUR grade (1–2,3,4–5), DMSA result with anatomical localization (upper pole, mid, lower, generalized), antibiotic prophylaxis agent (TMP-SMX, cephalexin, amoxicillin, nitrofurantoin, other), adherence (good/poor), bowel–bladder dysfunction (binary), comorbidities. Primary outcome: breakthrough febrile UTI while on continuous prophylaxis. Baselines: (1) unadjusted univariate associations; (2) baseline multivariable logistic regression with demographics only; (3) full multivariable logistic regression with all clinical predictors; (4) gradient-boosted classifier (XGBoost) for predictive comparison; (5) Cox proportional hazards model for time-to-first-breakthrough event. Causal comparisons: propensity-score matching (1:1 or 1:2 nearest neighbor, caliper 0.2 SD) and inverse-probability weighting to compare cephalexin vs TMP-SMX. Missing data: multiple imputation by chained equations (m=20). Variable selection: LASSO for parsimonious model; report full model coefficients. Evaluation metrics: adjusted odds ratios with 95% CI and p-values; AUC-ROC, calibration slope, Brier score, net reclassification index, decision-curve net benefit; hazard ratios for Cox models. Statistical tests: Wald tests and likelihood-ratio tests; significance threshold p<0.05. Ablation studies: (A) remove DMSA localization variables to quantify their incremental predictive value; (B) remove bowel–bladder dysfunction; (C) model excluding patients with poor adherence; (D) antibiotic-effect sensitivity: restrict to propensity-matched adherent subgroup. Report bootstrapped (n=1000) CIs for performance metrics and effect estimates. Risk Factors and Limitations: Observational design prevents definitive causal inference; residual confounding and confounding by indication for antibiotic choice are likely. Single-center, retrospective data spanning 2000–2019 may reflect temporal changes in antibiotic resistance and diagnostic practice, limiting generalizability. Modest sample size and limited number of breakthrough events (n≈86) constrain multivariable model degrees of freedom and increase risk of overfitting; rare-exposure effects (e.g., cephalexin subgroup) may produce wide CIs and unstable estimates. Measurement error: misclassification of UTI (culture availability, febrile vs afebrile), imperfect adherence assessment, and inter-reader variability in DMSA localization. Collinearity between VUR grade, renal scarring, and prior UTI burden may produce unstable coefficient estimates. Missing data patterns may be non-random. External validation may be unavailable. Statistical limitations include limited power to detect small-to-moderate effect sizes and to support complex machine-learning models. Computational requirements are modest but bootstrap and propensity analyses increase runtime.
